For team onboarding, this simplicity means the tool installs quickly, starts immediately, and doesn't require managing complex dependency trees. The trade-off is that SPACE implements more functionality from scratch than tools with richer dependency sets — but this is intentional, as it keeps the tool auditable and maintainable. For educators, the minimal dependencies make SPACE an excellent teaching tool for software supply chain security: 'Here's a real project with 0 production dependencies. Compare this with a typical React app that might have 1000+ dependencies. Which approach is more secure and why?' This exercise teaches students about dependency management, security auditing, and the cost-benefit trade-offs of the npm ecosystem.

5.2.4.ethicist: SPACE's versioning and compatibility policies determine how users experience updates and whether they're forced into changes they didn't choose. The current approach — supporting Node.js 18+ and modern browsers — excludes older environments, which is acceptable for a development tool but becomes an equity concern if the tool is used in educational settings with outdated lab hardware. The browser support policy (Chrome 90+, Firefox 90+, Edge 90+, Safari 15+) means students or developers using older browsers — often due to institutional IT policies that restrict browser updates — cannot use the web UI. The lack of a formal deprecation policy means that breaking changes in the Framework format could invalidate existing projects without warning. For organizations that have built internal processes around SPACE, this creates upgrade risk: a new version might change the question format, artifact schema, or export format in ways that break downstream tooling. The semantic versioning approach is a positive step, but without a documented compatibility matrix, users can't assess the risk of upgrading. An ethical versioning policy would include: guaranteed backward compatibility for project files (at least 2 major versions), a migration guide for every breaking change, and LTS (long-term support) versions for enterprise users.
5.2.4.futurist: SPACE's versioning model will evolve from simple semantic versioning to a multi-track versioning system within two years. The Framework format will be independently versioned from the tool: Framework v2.x can be loaded by Tool v3.x, enabling framework evolution without tool reinstallation. The project file format will gain explicit version metadata and automatic migration scripts, so upgrading the tool automatically migrates existing projects. Within five years, the versioning concept will be reframed as 'capability negotiation': when the tool loads a project, it will read the project's format version and enable/disable features accordingly, rather than requiring an exact version match. This enables forward compatibility (older projects work in newer tools) and backward compatibility (newer projects work in older tools, with graceful degradation). The browser support policy will adopt a 'latest 2 versions' rule rather than fixed version numbers, keeping pace with the rapid release cycles of modern browsers. The Node.js version policy will track the Node.js LTS schedule, supporting all currently maintained LTS versions. The dependency on Ollama for local AI will require a minimum version policy that tracks Ollama's feature evolution.
5.2.4.educator:
SPACE uses semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) and requires Node.js 18 or newer. For your team, the practical implications are: Node.js 18, 20, or 22 will work; older versions (16, 14) will not. The web UI requires Chrome 90+, Firefox 90+, Edge 90+, or Safari 15+ — these are browsers from mid-2021 or later. If your lab hardware has older browsers, the CLI interface is the fallback. For team onboarding, pin the Node.js version using nvm or fnm and the SPACE version using package.json: 'space@^1.0.0' ensures you get patches without breaking changes. When upgrading SPACE, check the CHANGELOG.md for breaking changes before updating — particularly changes to the Framework JSON format or the export schema. For educators, document the exact Node.js and browser versions in your lab documentation and test against them. Create a setup script that installs the correct versions: '#!/bin/bash
curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.39.0/install.sh | bash
nvm install 20
nvm use 20
npm install -g space-cli' — this ensures every student starts with the same environment.

5.2.5.ethicist: SPACE's build system simplicity — tsc for compilation, npm for packaging, GitHub Actions for CI/CD — reflects a commitment to transparency and reproducibility. Every build step is visible, every artifact is auditable, and every dependency is declared. The absence of complex bundlers (webpack, esbuild, Rollup) means there's no opaque transformation step between source and output — the compiled JavaScript is a direct translation of the TypeScript source. This transparency is ethically valuable for a tool that generates system specifications: users should be able to trust that the tool's output isn't influenced by hidden build-time transformations. However, the CI/CD pipeline's reliance on GitHub Actions ties the project's integrity to GitHub's infrastructure and policies. If GitHub's terms of service change, or if access to the repository is restricted (as has happened in geopolitically sensitive contexts), the build pipeline breaks. The npm registry dependency for distribution is similarly centralized — a single point of failure and control. For organizations that need guaranteed supply chain integrity, the tool should offer verifiable builds (reproducible builds with deterministic output hashes) and alternative distribution channels beyond npm.
5.2.5.futurist: SPACE's build system will evolve from tsc+GitHub Actions to a multi-stage pipeline with supply chain security features within two years. The pipeline will add: SLSA (Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts) compliance for build provenance, Sigstore for cryptographic signing of releases, and SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) generation for every build. The tsc compilation will be augmented by esbuild for production bundling (reducing the CLI's startup time by pre-compiling and tree-shaking), while the source build remains pure tsc for development. Within five years, the build system will support reproducible builds — deterministic compilation where the same source always produces byte-identical output, verifiable by third parties. The CI/CD will expand from GitHub Actions to a multi-platform pipeline that builds and tests on Linux, macOS, and Windows simultaneously, with automated release publishing to npm, Docker Hub, and a self-hosted package registry. The packaging format will evolve to include a single-file executable (via Node.js SEA or Bun compile) that eliminates the need for Node.js installation entirely, similar to how Go distributes single-binary tools.
5.2.5.educator: SPACE's build system is refreshingly simple: run 'tsc' to compile TypeScript to JavaScript, run 'npm pack' to create a distributable package. For team contributors, the development workflow is: clone the repo, run 'npm install' to get dev dependencies, run 'npm run build' to compile, and run 'npm test' to verify. The CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions) runs these same commands on every pull request, plus linting and type checking. No complex build configuration, no custom build scripts, no webpack configuration files. For onboarding new contributors, this simplicity is a major advantage: they can focus on understanding the code rather than wrestling with build tooling. The CI pipeline's output is visible on the GitHub Actions tab, making it easy to debug build failures. For educators, SPACE's build system teaches good practices through simplicity: TypeScript strict mode enforces type safety, vitest enforces test coverage, and the CI pipeline enforces that all checks pass before merging. Use this as a teaching example: 'This project has 3 build commands (build, test, lint) and a 20-line CI config. Compare this with your project's 15 build scripts and 200-line CI config. What can you simplify?'

5.3.1.ethicist: SPACE's performance model — single-user, synchronous, local-first — has ethical implications for who the tool serves and who it excludes. The <100ms response time for local operations creates an instant-feedback experience that supports thoughtful, deliberate specification writing. However, the single-session assumption means the tool fundamentally cannot support collaborative specification workflows, which are essential for equitable team participation. In organizations where specification responsibilities are distributed across team members with different schedules, time zones, or work arrangements, a single-session tool creates a bottleneck: only one person can work on the specification at a time. The 1-5 second LLM latency for auto-fill is acceptable for individual use but creates a significant time burden for users who need to auto-fill many questions sequentially. The throughput ceiling (limited by user input speed, not system capacity) is actually an ethical design choice — it prioritizes thoughtfulness over speed, ensuring that the specification reflects deliberate human decisions rather than batch-processed answers. However, for organizations that need to generate specifications quickly (incident response, rapid prototyping), the deliberately slow pace may be a barrier.
5.3.1.futurist: SPACE's current throughput model (one question at a time, synchronous processing) will be transformed by concurrent AI-assisted specification generation within three years. The system will maintain a background worker that continuously processes answers, extracts artifacts, and prepares follow-up questions — enabling the user to answer questions at their own pace while the system stays ahead of them. The latency profile will shift: local operations (question routing, answer recording) will remain sub-millisecond, but LLM operations will become async and batched, with results delivered via WebSocket push rather than synchronous HTTP response. Within five years, the throughput model will support parallel question tracks: users can answer questions from multiple Series simultaneously, with the AI maintaining consistency across parallel threads. The concurrency model will expand from single-user to collaborative: multiple team members will answer different questions concurrently, with the system merging their contributions and flagging conflicts. The performance requirement will shift from 'response time' to 'throughput per team member' — the metric that matters for collaborative specification is how quickly the team as a whole can produce a complete specification, not how quickly one person can answer one question.
5.3.1.educator: SPACE's performance is defined by three numbers: <100ms for local operations, 1-5 seconds for LLM auto-fill, and single-user concurrency. The local operations are effectively instant — you won't notice any delay when navigating questions, recording answers, or viewing artifacts. The LLM auto-fill runs in the background and doesn't block your interaction with the tool — you can continue answering questions while the AI processes previous ones. The single-user model means one person uses one session at a time — this is important for teams to understand, as concurrent access to the same session file could cause data corruption. For team workflows, each team member should work on their own session and export independently. For educators, SPACE's performance model is a teaching opportunity: the <100ms target for local operations teaches students about performance budgets. Ask them: 'What would you need to change to maintain <100ms if the question count grew from 326 to 3,260?' The answer (index-based lookup instead of linear scan, pre-computed progress states) teaches algorithm complexity in a practical context.
